title: Greenfield v. Philles Records, Inc.
summary: The same decision applied New York’s textual approach to a recording agreement and California’s contextual approach to a separate divorce release.
notes:
The plaintiffs were the Ronettes (Ronnie Greenfield, formerly Veronica Bennett, with Estelle Bennett and Nedra Talley); the 1963 agreement ran five years, produced recordings including "Be My Baby," and the disputed licensing for film and television began in the 1980s (Greenfield v. Philles Records, Inc., 98 N.Y.2d 562 (2002)).

Rule in one line: an unambiguous grant of full ownership of master recordings permits every use by the owner unless the contract expressly limits specific uses, and the artists cannot use extrinsic evidence to read in a limitation.

sections.Parties: The Ronettes sued Philles Records and Phil Spector over uses of their recordings and unpaid compensation. A separate issue concerned Ronnie Greenfield’s release of claims in her divorce settlement.
sections.Material Facts:
The group’s 1963 recording agreement required exclusive services and transferred ownership of the master recordings to Philles, with a royalty schedule. The ownership clause gave Philles the recordings and reproductions entirely, free of claims, and authorized reproduction by methods then known or later developed. The artists received an initial collective advance of about $15,000 and no later royalty payments.

Philles later licensed recordings for films and television, domestic redistribution, and compilation albums. The artists contended those particular uses were outside the grant because they were not specifically listed. Separately, Greenfield and Spector had exchanged general releases in a 1974 California divorce settlement. The defendants argued that her release eliminated her recording-related claims.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court awarded approximately $3 million, and the Appellate Division affirmed, using an industry royalty rate for uses it regarded as unauthorized. The New York Court of Appeals modified the order and remitted for further proceedings. It upheld the determination that Greenfield’s release did not eliminate her rights under the recording agreement.
sections.Issue: Did silence about particular later uses narrow an otherwise unconditional transfer of recording ownership, and did Greenfield’s general divorce release encompass recording royalties?
sections.Holding: The ownership grant covered the challenged uses subject to applicable royalty obligations. Under the California approach governing the release, extrinsic evidence supported exclusion of recording compensation from that release.
sections.Reasoning:
For the recording contract, the court applied New York’s rule that a complete, clear writing is enforced according to its terms. A broad grant of ownership need not enumerate every technological format or licensing method. Silence about a particular use did not create ambiguity when the ownership provision was otherwise unconditional. The court distinguished the right to exploit the recordings from the obligation to pay the royalties the contract required.

For the divorce release, California law permitted preliminary consideration of credible evidence of the parties’ intended scope. The lower courts’ finding that recording compensation was outside the intended release was supported by the record. Thus the same court reached different evidentiary treatment for two instruments because different substantive law applied.

The judgment did not approve withholding all royalties. It rejected the theory that the licensing uses were unauthorized merely because unlisted and required further proceedings on compensation consistent with the ownership grant.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It shows concretely why identifying the governing law precedes applying a general statement about contractual interpretation.

topics.interpretation: A broad ownership grant covered unlisted uses; the separate release was construed with context.
topics.assent: The scope of expressed agreement differs from an inventory of specifically anticipated applications.
topics.governing-law: New York and California rules governed different agreements in one dispute.
topics.parol-evidence: The court treated outside evidence differently for the two instruments.
topics.integration: New York's approach in the case enforces an unambiguous, complete writing by its four corners and excludes extrinsic evidence offered to add a use restriction, which is an integration analysis.
